name: Renaissance sacred polyphony (1450-1600)
lineage: Renaissance European sacred-music tradition c.1450-1600, the mass-cycle and motet repertoire of the Franco-Flemish and Italian schools. Canonical compositional features: imitative counterpoint with successive voice-entries on the same melodic subject; smooth melodic voice-leading with stepwise motion and small leaps; controlled dissonance through suspension-and-resolution; modal scales transitioning gradually into tonal practice; a cappella ideal with optional organ accompaniment for liturgical performance. Canonical composers: Josquin des Prez (Franco-Flemish, c.1450-1521, founding figure of the imitative-mass tradition); Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina (Roman, 1525-1594, Missa Papae Marcelli 1567 the Counter-Reformation touchstone for the smoothness-and-clarity ideal); Thomas Tallis (English, c.1505-1585, the forty-voice motet Spem in alium c.1570); William Byrd (English, c.1543-1623, Mass for Four Voices); Orlande de Lassus (Flemish, 1532-1594); Tomás Luis de Victoria (Spanish, 1548-1611). Geographical centers: Cambrai, Antwerp, Rome (Cappella Sistina), Venice (San Marco), London (Chapel Royal). Distinguished from medieval organum by full imitative counterpoint and tempered-meantone tuning vocabulary; distinguished from Baroque sacred polyphony by absence of basso continuo and absence of operatic-aria stylistic vocabulary; distinguished from Orthodox liturgical chant by Latin-text Roman-rite (vs Slavonic / Greek Orthodox-rite) liturgical framework
